sources: Green, Miranda. Symbol and Image in Celtic Religious Art. London: Routledge, 1989, 99.
Ross, Anne. Pagan Celtic Britain: Studies in Iconography and Tradition. London: Routledge & Kegan Paul, 1967, 30.

text: The genius loci is a Celtic god of the Continent and Britain. The Latin phrase means spirit of the place. These divinities embody special natural places. Such places include mountains, wells, waterfalls, and prominent glacial boulders. The Celts saw nature as full of divinity. Each god or goddess belonged to one site. Few divine names occur more than once. Rivers and mountains were usually goddesses. Trees and some streams were gods. Place-deities guided fertility, prosperity, and death in their region. Roman settlers affixed the names of their own gods to the native ones. This practice is called interpretatio romana. Apollo, Minerva, and Mercury stood in for many nature gods. Because altars read simply genius loci, many names were lost.
